cards.tip: FIX — When the system is healthy ("nothing's changed in three months"), don't walk away without offering the membership program or efficiency upgrades; after your diagnostic summary, pitch directly: "Great news—everything's running perfectly. Have you considered our service agreement that covers your next maintenance visits?"

FIX — When the customer said the WiFi 'reconnects pretty quick,' you should have presented it with pricing and urgency: 'That intermittent behavior means it's failing — we can replace the driver for $X now, or it'll fail completely in a few months and cost more for an emergency call,' then ask for the sale instead of leaving it open-ended.

FIX — When the customer wanted the estimate for that blower pull-and-clean, you should've asked directly 'Want us to take care of that now?' instead of framing it for the future — the direct ask is what closes the sale.

WIN — By measuring the subcool and explaining that 'it's not gonna be cold, it's gonna be more like lukewarm' with low refrigerant, Stanley identified the exact issue the customer was facing, which got them to approve the three-pound charge.

WIN — You built trust by confirming her unit's in excellent shape, then when you laid out the specific SAM benefits—winter plumbing check, 15% discount, emergency visit waiver—she said yes immediately; transparency about her system plus clear value proposition closed it.

FIX — After diagnosing the failing pump, when the customer showed they understood the problem, Matthew should have presented 3–4 specific repair options with pricing and asked 'Which option works for you?' in that moment, instead of deferring to an email report—because when the customer later cited the need for due diligence, the sale window had already closed.

FIX — When the customer mentioned getting a third opinion, you should have directly asked 'Which of these three options would you like to move forward with?' — getting them to commit to one option secures the decision before comparison shopping with other companies.

FIX — Customer proactively asked about maintenance, showing interest, but you need to present your repair or upgrade options first; run your full inspection and show 4-plus priced options during the diagnosis before taking the membership order.

WIN — When your customer asked if the membership meant you'd come check other things, you'd already shown 'it's a no-brainer': $312 in repair discounts against $192 annual membership cost—they went from hesitant to 'Yeah, why not?' because the numbers justified it.

FIX — When the customer mentioned the thermostat fan had been running continuously for 2 years, that was your opening to recommend a full system inspection or preventive maintenance package while you were already there—instead, you quickly adjusted the setting and moved on without exploring upgrade opportunities.

WIN — When Xavier presented the side-by-side cost comparison ($240 with membership and 15% future discounts versus $303 for just the part), the customer did the math and recognized the membership would pay for itself — they committed to the SAM signup.

FIX — When the customer expressed doubt about not getting a supervisor after two previous visits, that was the moment to reassure them and set clear expectations for what would make today different; the vague response didn't rebuild confidence.

WIN — Your clear diagnosis ('the wire is totally crisp...it probably could have been rubbed through and caused it to heat up') gave the customer confidence to approve the $264 repair immediately; when they said 'you're already here,' they signaled trust in your assessment.

FIX — When the customer said 'as long as we can just sleep tonight,' expressing worry about the new AC, you replied 'It hopefully should' instead of presenting 4+ options with pricing and offering the maintenance agreement—that conversation window is where the sale closes.

FIX — The customer confirmed systems were running normally with no complaints, which should have triggered the membership pitch and maintenance discussion; once the inspection confirms everything's working, circle back before leaving—'Your systems are running great and here's how we keep them that way with our SAM agreement'—even a maintenance call is a sales opportunity when you bring value through prevention, not just repair.

FIX — After the customer showed you the condensate line gunk and explained they'd cleaned it, that was your moment to say 'Good catch—once I finish inspecting, I'll show you a couple ways we can prevent that buildup and keep your system running efficiently'—that plants the seed for maintenance options before you present pricing.

FIX — After confirming the system's working well, present 4–6 repair/upgrade options with pricing, then ask for approval to proceed—you stopped after diagnosis and got into internal equipment talk instead of building the customer's menu to choose from.

WIN — After the successful test, you asked 'all I need from you now is $112—do you want to use one of the cards on file, or—' and the customer immediately agreed and paid; a direct ask right after proving the system works is your repeatable close for service calls.

FIX — Customer didn't object to your prices on the Vegas kit and switch replacement, but you jumped to email confirmation without asking 'Should I go ahead with both of these?'—get that approval before you leave.

FIX — When the customer indicated the system is loud, you started investigating with 'Is that your air filter?'—complete that diagnosis by explaining the cause, present 2-3 specific options with pricing (filter upgrade, coil cleaning, efficiency upgrade), and ask directly which solution works best for them.

FIX — After your clear capacitor diagnosis, the customer was ready to commit—instead of one $264 quote, say 'We can do the capacitor for $264 alone, or add our maintenance plan to prevent this again'—presenting options up front gets the yes before the landlord objection.

WIN — Customer expressed concern about being caught without AC in 107-degree heat and having to pay for a hotel during emergency repair. Tech reframed the upgrade as preventive: 'That's why we offer stuff like this, so we can try to avoid things like that.' Tech validated the customer's own logic rather than pushing, letting the customer reach the conclusion to buy.

FIX — Customer described ongoing temperature balance issues; you checked the system and found it in spec, but never presented upgrade options (maintenance membership, zoning adjustment) or asked for their business—missing the chance to close a sale or at minimum get clear approval to proceed.

FIX — When the customer said 'you're the professional, I don't know what options I need'—step in with 2–3 clear scenarios (minimal/recommended/comprehensive) and ask directly 'which one works best to get you to 100% today?'—that advisory close would have locked it down instead of it floating on a pending email.

FIX — When the customer signaled affordability constraints ('if we can afford it now'), ask what they CAN afford today and build a solution at that price point—Matthew presented one option and scheduled for later, leaving the real objection unresolved.

WIN — She said she'd been charged at the old house and wouldn't sign anything else; you went to your boss and came back with 'I told him and he's putting a note on your account'—that ownership took her from walking away to signed membership.

FIX — After your evaluation, you went straight to technical voltage and wiring details instead of circling back with distinct repair options and pricing—customers need to see choices first, so they know what to approve and what it costs.

FIX — When the customer asked to review the summary before deciding, Jose should have offered the minimum repair option as a starting point—something like 'Let me send you those details, but let's secure the compressor and fan motor work today to protect your system'—to lock in a sale rather than defer the entire job.

FIX — When the customer said 'I don't think I can do it today,' ask 'Is it timing or budget that's the concern?' instead of just saying 'that's fine, we'll send emails'—the customer was already bought into the microprocessor upgrade benefits, but you needed one probing question to either close it or lock in a next-visit commitment.

WIN — when the customer mentioned weak airflow to two bedrooms, showing them the heavily dusty filter side-by-side with the clean one and explaining 'the filter could cause airflow restrictions' made them agree to the change immediately.

WIN — Your honest answer on component options—'we don't really offer handless on commercials'—showed the experienced customer you wouldn't oversell them; that transparent expertise is what earns trust on commercial accounts and led to the direct approval.

FIX — When you offered the maintenance program and got 'I'll think about it,' you accepted the deferral without a direct ask. Counter with: 'How about we start with one month free so we monitor that sound during maintenance visits—if it's serious, we fix it in warranty at no charge.' That's the ask that turns hesitation into commitment.

WIN — When Stanley offered to waive the $39 first-month fee ('if you sign up, I can wait that $39'), the customer immediately committed ('Yeah, I actually wanted to sign up because we don't have a service'), proving the sale hinged on removing the final friction point.

FIX — When the customer asked 'how does this sound?' on the outdoor unit, that was the moment to present a diagnostic and repair option, but you only noted the problem instead of selling the solution.

FIX — Customer brought up 'he quoted you for the air scrubber for the allergies'—you said 'Yeah' but pivoted to water explanation instead of asking 'Want me to get you pricing on that scrubber?' and closing it; the direct upsell with cost was the missing move.

WIN — When the customer expressed time pressure to leave by 6 for an event, J Boothe said 'I enjoy the chatting. I just don't want to make you late'—balancing genuine connection with respect for their schedule; the customer then called it 'a very easy transaction' and credited J with making 'the day go nice,' proving that authentic engagement is what earned approval without sales friction.

FIX — When the customer confirmed understanding of the switch issue ('it's probably the one that's tied to these 2 thermostats?'), that was your moment to convert: 'Since you have less than a year on warranty and this switch is showing failure signs, I'd recommend we replace it now for [price] to avoid a no-cool emergency — shall we get that scheduled?' Instead you said 'something to think about,' and the customer left without approving either repair.

FIX — When customers heard about the voltage switch corrosion and high amperage issues, they were engaged but Juan said 'I just don't want the next tech to come and be like, hey, did they ever bring this up to your attention?' instead of presenting a structured menu of 4+ options with pricing and asking directly 'Which option works for you?'—missing both the options presentation and the close.

FIX — When the customer asked 'How much is that gonna be?' and then said 'let me talk to my wife about it,' you needed to test that buying signal ('Does $1,877 work for your budget?') and then ask directly: 'Perfect—let me get you scheduled for [date], so once you two decide we can get started right away,' instead of leaving it to them to call back.
